title: Dodgers' three-peat dream dies with Game 4 NLCS loss to Brewers | United States
text:
Shohei Ohtani erupted with an early home run, but the Milwaukee Brewers rallied to beat the Dodgers and sweep the NLCS Thursday at Dodger Stadium.
Dodgers Miguel Rojas, Tommy Edman and catcher Hunter Feduccia stand in the dugout during Game 4 of the NLCS at Dodger Stadium on Thursday. Shohei Ohtani’s three-run homer briefly revived the crowd, but the Brewers rallied to erase the advantage.
The Dodgers put runners at third in three consecutive innings but couldn’t bring them home, sealing the end of a three-peat dream.briefly stoked the flame. But it already had been snuffed out by the time the final out landed in Brewers left fielder Jackson Chourio’s glove. The Dodgers’ hopes of making National League history with a three-peat died with a 6-4 loss to the Brewers on Thursday, completing Milwaukee’s four-game sweep.
As the Dodgers’ postseason hype video declared before the game: “October doesn’t remember who came close. It remembers who triumphs. ”The Dodgers, after reinforcing their roster from back-to-back championships in the offseason and entering the year as the World Series favorites, were swept out of the NLCS by the team they did it to last year. When they went down 3-0 in the series, they faced a steep climb that only one team in MLB history has overcome.
But the Dodgers showed resolve to begin the game.driving in the first run. It was his third hit of the postseason with runners in scoring position and the Dodgers’ fourth overall.
Then with two outs, Ohtani not only prolonged the inning but also made it the Dodgers’ highest-scoring frame of the postseason, with their first home run of the series. It had been a maddening couple of months as Ohtani battled injuries, slid down the batting order and failed to produce when the Dodgers needed him most — in the postseason. Plaschke: The Dodgers had everything needed to three-peat.
This is why they failed The Dodgers were attempting to become the first team in NL history to win three straight championships. Bill Plaschke questions why they failed. Ohtani turned to the Dodgers’ dugout, spread his arms wide and tossed his bat to the side. He tilted his face to the sky and yelled.
He punched the air. This was the version of Ohtani the Dodgers had sorely been missing. He announced his return with authority. And he breathed life into a stadium that had a crowd of only 49,104 — short of a sellout.
It was his first home run since Aug. 18. And it had been even longer since he’d hit a homer quite like that. With an exit velocity of 113.1 mph, it was his hardest-hit home run since June 20 and his third-hardest hit of the year, according to Statcast.kept the good vibes going, retiring the first 10 batters he faced. But the Brewers, as they had all series, had a comeback in them.
It began with one out in the fourth inning, as Brice Turang drew a walk, the first baserunner against Glasnow. Then William Contreras and Jake Bauers each bounced ground-rule doubles into the stands, Bauers’ driving in two runs to cut the Dodgers’ lead in half. The next inning, the Brewers used a walk, a stolen base and David Hamilton’s single to tie the score and knock Glasnow out of it.
Then, in the sixth, Dodgers setup man Tanner Scott took the mound early, at an inflection point in the contest. He worked ahead 0-and-2 in the count to Garrett Mitchell. But Mitchell spat on three straight balls to get to a full count. Scott missed down the middle with a fastball.
Mitchell sent it over the fence to give the Brewers the lead for the first time.moved him over with a groundout. In the seventh, Pages led off with a double, and Kiké Hernández bunted him over. In the eighth, with one out, Will Smith cut out the middle man by doubling into the right-field corner and advancing to third when Milwaukee’s Sal Frelick misplayed the carom off the wall.
The Dodgers stranded all three at third, failing to score the tying run. Max Muncy struck out in the sixth; Ohtani struck out and Mookie Betts grounded out in the seventh; and Tucker popped out and Teoscar Hernández struck out in the eighth. Díaz did his part to keep the Dodgers in the game, retiring eight straight batters in the longest appearance of his career.
But the ninth batter he faced, Hamilton, hit a solo homer to cushion the Brewers’ lead. Maddie Lee covers the Dodgers for the Los Angeles Times. She joined the paper in March 2026 after six years in Chicago, where she was a Cubs beat writer for the Chicago Sun-Times and NBC Sports Chicago. Her previous stops include the Oklahoman, the Clarion-Ledger, the Salt Lake Tribune and the Owensboro Messenger-Inquirer.
